support.corpus: Old English poetry (Beowulf, Gutenberg; Grein 1857-58, OCR)

cognate: The *gʷʰen- 'slay' word: Ved. han- (áhan, jaghāna, ghnán) ~ OE bana/bona, ON bani 'slayer' (*gʷʰon-, pie-lex-gwhonox). The Germanic anchor (Beo. 2903) supplies only the context and the renewed serpent noun (wyrm). The cognate agent noun is attested in search support from the same episode (Beo. 2825 'Bona ... eorð-draca ... wyrm') and in Hymiskviða 22 'orms einbani', which is my reading of the OCR 'eiribani'.
drift_or_renewal: The serpent noun is renewed in Germanic: OE wyrm / ON ormr (*wr̥mi- 'worm, larva', cf. Lat. uermis) and draca replace *h₁ogʷʰi-; the inherited verb survives as the agent noun *gʷʰonō 'slayer' (bana/bani) rather than as a finite verb. Germanic also keeps the variant where the serpent kills the hero (Beowulf dead 'wyrmes dǣdum', Thor walking nine steps from the serpent and dying), which Watkins counts as part of the same theme (recalled).
shared_syntax: Ved.: verb + accusative object (áhim han-, 'slew the serpent'); Gmc.: genitive object + agent noun ('orms einbani' = 'the serpent's sole slayer'), i.e. the same verb-object pairing nominalised.
context: Same mythic scene in both: a champion (Indra; Beowulf; Thor, 'Óðins sonr') fights and kills a unique monstrous serpent. RV 1.32.4a is Indra's slaying of the firstborn of serpents; Beo. 2903 is the report of the Geat lord lying dead by the dragon's deeds after killing it, and Beo. 2825 (same episode) calls the dragon 'bona' as it lies dead beside him; Hym. 22 names Thor 'orms einbani' as he fishes for the Miðgarð serpent. The pairing of a *gʷʰen- word with the serpent in Germanic, where 'kill' is normally drepa/slean/cwellan, is not generic. The packet's non:Skýringar 7 [edda:19841] ('bani') is Finnur Jónsson's modern Icelandic commentary to Völuspá 53-55, not Eddic text, so I do not anchor on it.
phrase: *gʷʰen- *h₁ógʷʰim 'slay the serpent' (pie-lex-gwhenti + pie-lex-h1ogwhis); Gmc. renewal *wurmiz/ *wr̥mi- + *gʷʰonō 'serpent's slayer'

cognate: Lat. anguis and Ved. áhi- are usually treated as variants of one serpent word (*h₂engʷʰi- / *h₁ogʷʰi-, with Lith. angìs, Gk ὄφις, ἔχις; recalled). The lexicon keeps them as two entries (pie-lex-h2engwhis vs pie-lex-h1ogwhis), so the noun is a near-cognate at best.
drift_or_renewal: The verb is renewed in Latin: uincere (1123) and enicare (1119) take the place of *gʷʰen-, which Latin keeps only in compounds of -fendo (defendo). Greek keeps *gʷʰen- in this theme for Heracles (Eur. HF 1275 ὕδραν φονεύσας) and Perseus (Pind. P. 10.46 ἔπεφνεν Γοργόνα), but with renewed monster names.
shared_syntax: Verb + accusative serpent object (anguis uicerit / ambo anguis enicat ~ áhim jaghāna).
context: Bromia tells how the infant Hercules, son of Jupiter (summus imperator diuom), sprang from the cradle and killed two serpents, and Jupiter names him as the one 'qui illas anguis uicerit'. The hero killing a serpent, with the hero tied to the sky-god, matches Indra slaying Ahi. The theme is inherited (Watkins, recalled), but the Plautine wording is comic narration rather than formulaic diction, and the verb is renewed, so the link rests on the theme and the noun.
phrase: *gʷʰen- *h₁ógʷʰi-/*h₂éngʷʰi- 'slay the serpent', with Latin renewal of the verb (uincere/enicare anguis)

cognate: *n̥-mr̥tó- 'immortal' as the standing epithet and substitute for 'gods': Ved. amŕ̥ta- (RV 7.4.5b amŕ̥tān = the gods; devā́ amŕ̥tāḥ is frequent, 23 RV pādas) ~ Gk ἄμβροτος (θεὸς ἄμβροτος, Il. 24.460, Il. 22.9; recalled as an exact equation). Its counterpart is *mr̥tó-/*mórto- 'mortal' = humans: Ved. márta- (RV 6.16.32c) ~ Gk βροτός (Od. 1.66). Lat. deus ~ Ved. devá- (the Greek god word θεός is not cognate).
drift_or_renewal: Greek usually renews ἄμβροτος as ἀθάνατος in this slot (Od. 1.67 θεοῖσιν ἀθανάτοισιν, the context line after the anchor) and keeps ἄμβροτος mostly for divine substances. Latin immortalis is a fresh formation (-āli-) on mort-, not the old *-tó- adjective. Both renewals are formally transparent, which is why the slot survives.
shared_syntax: Noun 'god(s)' + attributive 'immortal' (devā́ amŕ̥tāḥ ~ θεὸς ἄμβροτος ~ dii immortales), or the adjective used alone for 'gods', opposed to 'mortals' (márta- ~ βροτοί ~ mortales).
context: Od. 1.66-67 sets the wisdom of mortals (βροτῶν) against the sacrifices to the immortal gods. RV 7.4.5b has Agni passing beyond the immortals (amŕ̥tān), and RV 6.16.32c speaks of the hostile mortal (mártaḥ) who would kill us. Cato's 'dii immortales' opens his account of the gods' gift to the tribune, set against those lying 'inter mortuos'. The gods/mortals polarity defined by death is the same in all three. The packet's Av. VS12.22a mərətō means 'dead', not 'mortal', so I leave it out. The Latin is the weakest leg, because immortalis is not the inherited form.

words: summus imperator diuom atque hominum Iuppiter

cognate: Exact on both words and in the vocative case: Ved. dyaùḥ pítar (vocative with the irregular nominative-form dyaùḥ) = Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ = Lat. Iū-piter (univerbated vocative, the base of the Latin name; Umbr. Iupater, recalled).
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek. In Latin the vocative has fused into a proper name (Iuppiter), used for every case.
shared_syntax: Vocative of the sky-god's name + vocative 'father', opening a prayer (address + imperative/optative request).
context: RV 6.51.5a invokes 'Father Heaven, Mother Earth' to be kind and protect; Il. 17.645 (Ajax: 'Father Zeus, save the sons of the Achaeans from the mist') and Il. 7.179 (the army's prayer at the casting of lots) are prayers of request to the sky-father, and Theognis 731 is a wish addressed to him. Same speech act, same case, same order. Recalled: this is the textbook equation; the packet really contains it, and it is the only vocative dyaùḥ pítar in the RV (search: 8 RV pādas pair dyú- with pitár-, 41 Homeric lines have Ζεῦ ... πάτερ).

cognate: 'Mother' (*méh₂tēr) is exact in Indo-Iranian, Greek and Latin, and 'father' and the sky-god (*dyéws) in Ved./Gk/Lat. 'Earth' as 'the Broad One' (*pl̥th₂-), Ved. pr̥thivī́, has a cognate only in Germanic, OE folde (lexicon *pl̥th₂ós; e.g. Grein II Htmhen l.20678 'settest on foldan', which has no 'mother'). The OE charm pairing 'folde, fira modor' (Æcerbot) is recalled and is not in the local corpus.
drift_or_renewal: The earth word is renewed outside Indo-Iranian: Gk χθών (Hes. Th. 284), γαῖα/γῆ (support); Lat. terra/tellus (Lucretius). The sky partner is renewed as Οὐρανός (Hes. Th. 45, Pind. O. 7.38) or aether (Lucr. 1.250) next to the inherited Zeus/Dyaus/Iuppiter. Such renewal within a stable pairing is expected, and the inherited 'mother' keeps the formula visible.
shared_syntax: Coordinated pair or parallel nominal clauses 'Sky (is) father, Earth (is) mother' (dyaúḥ pitā́ pr̥thivī́ mātā́; Pater aether ... Matris terrai; omnibus ille idem Pater ... Mater terra), plus the appositional or vocative 'Earth mother' (pŕ̥thivi mā́tar RV 6.51.5a ~ ὦ γαῖα μῆτερ, Γᾶ μᾶτερ; χθόνα μητέρα).
context: In both branches the pair is the cosmic parent couple who are invoked for protection and blessing (RV 1.191.6a; RV 1.89.4b; AV 3.23.s14 'whose father is Dyaus, mother Pṛthivī' of the plants; AV 12.1.s26 'Earth is mother, I am Earth's son, Parjanya is father'). Hes. Th. 284 calls Earth 'mother of flocks', and the Greek and Latin support makes Earth the mother partnered with Sky: Pind. O. 7.38 Οὐρανός ... Γαῖα μάτηρ; Lucr. 1.250 Pater aether ... Matris terrai; Lucr. 2.992 Pater ... Mater terra. The vocative 'pŕ̥thivi mā́tar' of RV 6.51.5a matches Eur. Hipp. 601 ὦ γαῖα μῆτερ and Soph. Phil. 391 Γᾶ μᾶτερ. Other packet passages fit the theme but do not carry the pairing, so they are not anchors: Hes. Th. 45 (Gaia and Ouranos beget the gods); HH Bacch. 2 (Zeus and Semele as Dionysus' parents; Semele = 'earth' is a recalled, disputed Thraco-Phrygian etymology, and the lexicon's mapping to *dʰéǵʰōm is unverified); Lucr. 2.615 (the Magna Mater passage, where mater = tellus, 2.598ff). Recalled: Sky-Father/Earth-Mother is standard in comparative work (West, IEPM), but Earth-Mother is less securely reconstructable than Sky-Father.
phrase: *dyéws ph₂tḗr ... *pl̥th₂éwih₂ (or renewed 'Earth') méh₂tēr 'Father Sky, Mother Earth'

cognate: ON áss (< *ansuz) and Ved. ásura- are derivatives of one root (*h₂ens-u-, lexicon pie-lex-h2emsus / pie-root-h2ems); ON sonr = Ved. sūnú-.
drift_or_renewal: In the Vedic phrase 'son' is renewed (putrá- for sūnú-), and the head noun is the -ra- derivative ásura- (singular, 'the Lord', i.e. Dyaus), where ON has the plain u-stem in the plural ('the Æsir').
shared_syntax: Genitive of the divine-lord word + plural 'sons' as a collective name for a divine company (ása synir ~ putrā́saḥ ásurasya).
context: Both name a group of gods by descent from the divine Lord or Lords: in Lokasenna 64 'fyr ásum, fyr ása sonum' (Loki speaking before the gods); in RV 3.53.7/10.67.2 the Aṅgirases or Maruts are 'sons of Heaven, heroes of the Asura'. The packet's own Vedic anchor (RV 10.132.4a, voc. asura next to dyaúḥ) has only the lord word, not the phrase, so the parallel rests on searched support. 'Sons of god(s)' is a generic notion, so this is weak.

note: No defensible cross-branch parallel. The Vedic block is praise vocabulary (vā́c-, mánas-, √stu-, √vac-, stóma-, takṣ- vā́c in RV 9.97.22a), and its only near-partner, Avestan vacah-/tašta, is in the same branch. Greek has κρατερὴ ὑσμίνη, θάρσει and ἔχω phrases with no Vedic match. Germanic has OE māðmas geaf ~ ON meiðma þiggja, which is Germanic-internal. Latin has aurum atque argentum, dies noctesque and lux/lumen, with no partner in another branch here. Baltic has Latvian dainas about sowing flax. Possible leads I rejected: Lat. 'diem aquam solem lunam noctem' (PlAsina 198) against Ved. 'apáḥ svàr uṣásaḥ' (RV 6.60.2b), where only sōl ~ svàr is cognate and the context (nature's free goods vs. gods winning the waters and sun) is not congruent; Lat. aurora ... lumine (Lucr. 2.144) against Ved. uṣás ... śocíṣā (RV 1.48.14c), dawn and light, which is too generic. Pind. P. 10.46 ἔπεφνεν Γοργόνα and Eur. Phoen. 1507 Σφιγγὸς ... φονεύσας are useful as support for the monster-slaying claim in P-88ab but have no partner inside this packet.
